title: Family of Guelph man killed by police says he was 'deeply loved'
article: The family of a Guelph man killed in a police shooting incident last month says Brandon Duncan was someone "deeply loved by many."
Relatives of the 36-year-old issued a statement through a Toronto-based lawyer.

"We are devastated by the loss of our son, brother, grandson, nephew, cousin and friend," the statement begins. "We would like to sincerely thank all of the people who have provided us with an incredible groundswell of love and support since his tragic death."
The DLA Piper office of lawyer Mike Richards released the statement Saturday. It contained few details about Duncan's life or death, but offered a clarification about his burial.

"Brandon's body was claimed by his family immediately upon its release by the authorities," the statement asserts. "He was remembered and honoured at a memorial service last Tuesday, attended by more than 150 family, friends and support workers. Brandon was deeply loved by many."
It is unknown where the memorial service was held.

In the statement the family requested privacy as it deals with the tragic loss, stating that it would have no comment about the circumstances of his death until the Special Investigations Unit inquiry was complete and its findings released.

Since the May 20 shooting death of Duncan in the emergency department of the Guelph General Hospital, no details about his funeral arrangements or burial were released. The SIU, which is probing the police-involved death, declined to divulge information about the final arrangements for Duncan.

Silence on the issue prompted a local United Church minister Anne Gajerski-Cauley to organize a memorial in Guelph, which is scheduled for Thursday at 7 p.m. Wall-Custance Funeral Home and Chapel at 206 Norfolk St. in Guelph has donated space for the service. Gajerski-Cauley said in an email that planning for the memorial is going well.

On Monday, 40 Baker Street, an agency that houses programs for residents living in poverty, dedicated its Monday pizza supper to Duncan. 40 Baker co-ordinator Ed Pickersgill said just over 90 people attended.
"I didn't know him," said Erika Kropf, a former mental health worker who now works with children with autism. "I just wanted to show my respect for the victim of this tragedy."

Duncan was known to have accessed services for the homeless in Guelph for about 15 years, according to those who knew him. He suffered from mental illness and addiction, and was debilitated by Crohn's disease, a condition he had several surgeries for, Guelph associates have said.

Guelph resident Lesley Dickieson recounted in a recent report how she met Duncan one evening last November in a bank lobby as he struggled with a broken colostomy bag. He was desperate, homeless, and in pain. She helped the man, calmed him down, and called emergency medical services to get him to the hospital.

"He was obviously suffering a great deal," Kropf added. "He was a person who seemed to be in a lot of physical and emotional pain, and our community failed him. He did not get the supports he needed."

She said it is her hope that Duncan's death will result in enhanced training for police on how to deal with people with mental health problems. She added that expanding security at the hospital is not the answer, and will only intimate those who are in a mental health crisis.
"There has to be more attention paid to the needs of people like Brandon," she said. "A huge security force will deter them from getting the medical help they need."
Pickersgill said those who have to "follow the same path as Brandon" and access the emergency department for care, are anxious and fearful.

"They're concerned that now if you go to the ER one of the things that might happen is you might get shot if you don't behave yourself," he said. "People are not happy about that, they're nervous about that, and they don't know what to say about that. It is not good for the mental health of a troubled community."

Duncan was in the emergency department on the early afternoon of Wednesday, May 20. Police were called to the scene at around 1:30 p.m. Witnesses at the scene said they saw a woman bleeding and screaming outside the hospital after she fled through a set of doors.

The SIU reported that Duncan was shot multiple times in an "interaction" with two Guelph Police officers. Cellphone photographs taken by a bystander show Duncan face-first on a tiled floor, blood pooling around the right side of his body. He was wearing grey sweatpants and a T-shirt with the number '1' on the back.
One of those photographs along with a portrait photograph of Duncan was on display at the 40 Baker Street event on Monday. People were invited to write in a comment book.

Pickersgill said he hopes it matters to the broader community "that someone was shot at the Guelph General by two police officers." He believes the situation could have and should have been handled differently.

"But it wasn't. It was handled the way it was handled and Brandon is dead," he said. "I would hope that the mainstream community would take note of this and not be happy with it, and make some statements that might result in change."
